To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
D3KO mice have impaired clearance of T3 and that this leads to defects at the levels of hypothalamus, anterior pituitary and thyroid gland, which together cause central hypothyroid-like phenotype.
mice with a genetic deficiency of the enzyme D3 develop perinatal thyroid hyperactivity followed in adulthood by an apparent central hypothyroid state.
mice lacking the type 3 de-iodinase (a selenoenzymes that inactivates T(3)) develop perinatal hyperthyroidism and, later in life, central hypothyroid-like features.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the mechanisms by which thyroid hormone (T(3)) is inactivated in the central nervous system and the role of this process in the development of the nervous system.
the regulation of the mammalian thyroid axis.
the role of the type 3 de-iodinase (DI3) in the regulation of the hypothalamo-pituitary-thyroid axis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
D3 is a key component in the regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and its disruption results in a complex pattern of abnormalities at all levels of the axis.
D3KO mice are not only hypothyroid but also hyperthyroid.
D3 is a key enzyme for the maintenance of thyroid homeostasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
D3KO mice have a central hypothyroid phenotype.
D3KO mice have a thyroid hormone resistance syndrome.
type 3 deidoinase deficiency is a disease that results in functional abnormalities of the thyroid axis that are present from early development through adulthood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
D3 is a key component in the maintenance of thyroid homeostasis.
the D3 is not only a critical regulator of the thyroid hormone levels in the periphery but is also essential for the appropriate regulation of the thyroid hormone axis.
the thyroid axis is exquisitely sensitive to the level of circulating thyroid hormone, and even small differences in circulating T(3) can have significant effects on the thyroid axis.
